title: Genetics & Heredity — From Mendel to Molecular Biology

subChunks.title: Genetics & Heredity — From Mendel to Molecular Biology

storyBeats.txt: Theodora unrolled a diagram of a pea plant, its flower carefully dissected. "Gregor Mendel," she said, "spent seven years crossing pea plants in an Austrian monastery garden, counting tens of thousands of offspring. He saw patterns in the inheritance of flower colour, seed shape, and pod colour — patterns that pointed to discrete units of heredity. He published his findings in 1866. The world ignored them for thirty-four years."

"When Mendel's work was rediscovered in 1900, biologists had just found chromosomes — thread-like structures in the nucleus that doubled and separated during cell division. By 1902, Sutton and Boveri noticed that chromosomes behaved exactly like Mendel's hypothetical factors. The physical basis of heredity was beginning to come into view."

"Half a century later, Watson and Crick revealed the double helix, and suddenly both the storage and transmission of genetic information made chemical sense. Today we can read the complete sequence of a human genome in days, edit individual base pairs with molecular scissors, and trace the migrations of ancient human populations from traces of DNA extracted from 50,000-year-old bones. The story Mendel started with his pea plants has become one of the most consequential in the history of science."

subChunks.hookHtml: Genetics is the science of heredity — how traits are passed from parents to offspring and how the information encoded in DNA is used to build and maintain living organisms. From Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment to the molecular mechanisms of DNA replication, transcription, and translation, genetics has transformed biology from a descriptive to a predictive and engineering science. Modern genomics can sequence billions of base pairs, identify disease-causing mutations, and reconstruct evolutionary history from genetic data.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Mendel's Laws

Key terminology: Gene — a segment of DNA encoding a functional product. Allele — a specific version of a gene. Genotype — the alleles an organism carries. Phenotype — the observable characteristics. Homozygous — two identical alleles (AA or aa). Heterozygous — two different alleles (Aa). Dominant (A) — expressed in one or two copies. Recessive (a) — expressed only in homozygous recessive (aa).

Law of Segregation: Each organism has two alleles for each gene; these separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries one allele. Random fertilisation produces the Mendelian ratios.

Law of Independent Assortment: Alleles of different genes assort independently during gamete formation (applies to genes on different chromosomes). A dihybrid cross (AaBb × AaBb) gives a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.

Punnett squares: Grid method for calculating genotypic/phenotypic ratios. Monohybrid cross Aa × Aa → 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa = 3 dominant : 1 recessive phenotypic ratio.

Extensions to Mendelian Genetics

Incomplete dominance: Heterozygous phenotype is intermediate. Example: red (RR) × white (WW) → pink (RW) flowers.

Codominance: Both alleles fully expressed. Example: AB blood type — both A and B antigens present (I^A I^B genotype).

Multiple alleles: More than two alleles exist in the population (though any individual has only two). Blood group ABO system has three alleles: I^A, I^B, i.

Polygenic inheritance: Many genes contribute to a single phenotype (e.g. skin colour, height, IQ). Produces a continuous normal distribution rather than discrete categories.

Epistasis: One gene masks or modifies the expression of another. Complicates predicted ratios.

Chromosomes and Linkage

Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs): 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male). Genes on the same chromosome are linked — they tend to be inherited together rather than assorting independently. Crossing over (recombination) during meiosis shuffles alleles between homologous chromosomes, generating new combinations. Recombination frequency is used to map gene positions on chromosomes (genetic maps).

Sex-linked inheritance: Genes on the X chromosome — males (XY) have only one copy; a recessive X-linked allele is expressed in males. Examples: red-green colour blindness, haemophilia. X-linked recessive conditions are more common in males. Carrier females (X^A X^a) are phenotypically normal but can pass the allele to sons.

DNA, Genes, and the Genome

The human genome contains ≈3 × 10⁹ base pairs encoding ≈20,000–25,000 protein-coding genes, but only ≈2% of the genome codes for protein. The rest includes regulatory sequences, introns, repetitive elements, and sequences whose function is still being discovered.

Mutations: Changes in the DNA sequence. Point mutations (single base changes): silent (same amino acid), missense (different amino acid), nonsense (stop codon). Insertions/deletions cause frameshifts — disrupt the reading frame and usually abolish protein function. Chromosomal mutations: deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations.

Sources of mutation: Spontaneous errors in DNA replication (proofreading reduces error rate to ≈10⁻⁹ per base per replication). Mutagens: radiation (UV → thymine dimers; ionising radiation → strand breaks), chemical mutagens (intercalating agents, base analogues).

Gene Expression — From DNA to Protein

The Central Dogma: DNA → (transcription) → mRNA → (translation) → protein.

Gene regulation: Not all genes are expressed in all cells at all times. In prokaryotes, the lac operon is a classic example: genes encoding enzymes for lactose metabolism are transcribed only when lactose is present and glucose is absent. In eukaryotes, transcription factors, enhancers, silencers, chromatin remodelling, and epigenetic modifications (methylation, histone acetylation) regulate which genes are expressed in which cell types — explaining how a liver cell and a neuron have the same DNA but very different functions.

Biotechnology Applications

PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): Amplifies specific DNA sequences exponentially. Essential for diagnostics (COVID-19 tests), forensics (DNA profiling), and research.

Gel electrophoresis: Separates DNA fragments by size through a gel matrix in an electric field — basis of DNA profiling and diagnostic tests.

CRISPR-Cas9: A bacterial immune system repurposed as a precise molecular editing tool. A guide RNA directs the Cas9 nuclease to cut a specific sequence; the cell's repair machinery can be exploited to insert, delete, or replace sequences. Applications include treating genetic diseases, engineering crops, and basic research.

Genome sequencing: The Human Genome Project (completed 2003) sequenced the first reference human genome. Today, whole-genome sequencing costs ≈$200–500 and takes hours. Clinical genomics is increasingly central to personalised medicine.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what dominant and recessive alleles actually mean at the molecular level — why does having just one copy of a dominant allele produce the dominant phenotype?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is caused by a recessive allele (f) of the CFTR gene; the dominant allele (F) produces normal CFTR protein. Two carrier parents (Ff × Ff) have children. (1) Draw the Punnett square and calculate the probability of each possible genotype. (2) What is the probability that a child has CF? (3) What is the probability that a child is a carrier but unaffected? (4) If the family has four children, none of whom have CF, what is the probability that all four are carriers? (5) The parents have a CF-affected child. They want to know the probability that their next child will also have CF. Explain why the answer is not affected by how many children they have already had.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Punnett square (Ff × Ff): FF (25%), Ff (50%), ff (25%). Genotypic ratio 1:2:1.

(2) P(CF) = P(ff) = 25% = 0.25. One in four children on average will have CF.

(3) P(carrier, unaffected) = P(Ff) = 50% = 0.50. Note: of the unaffected children (FF + Ff = 75%), two-thirds are carriers (Ff/0.75 = 2/3 ≈ 67%).

(4) P(carrier | unaffected) for each child = P(Ff) / P(unaffected) = 0.50 / 0.75 = 2/3. P(all four unaffected children are carriers) = (2/3)⁴ = 16/81 ≈ 19.8%. This assumes each child's genotype is independent.

(5) The probability that the next child has CF is still 25% — independent of all previous births. Each conception is an independent event: sperm and egg randomly carry either F or f allele regardless of what happened before. The common misconception ("we've had one CF child so we're less likely to have another") is the gambler's fallacy — past random events do not alter future probabilities. Mendel's Law of Segregation applies anew at every fertilisation. This is why genetic counselling is crucial: even families who have had CF children face the same 25% risk with every subsequent pregnancy.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive condition caused by a deficient clotting factor VIII. (1) A carrier woman (X^H X^h) has children with a normal man (X^H Y). Calculate the probability of haemophilia in (a) all children, (b) sons only, (c) daughters only. (2) Explain why haemophilia is far more common in males than females. Under what genotypic condition would a female be affected? (3) Queen Victoria was a carrier of haemophilia A and passed it to several of her children who married into European royal families. Explain how Victoria could have been a carrier given that neither of her parents showed signs of haemophilia. Propose two possible genetic explanations. (4) A new mutation arises in a non-carrier family, causing haemophilia A in a son. Through which parent and which gamete did this mutation most likely arise? Explain. (5) A girl is born with haemophilia A. What does this tell you about her genotype, and therefore what must be true about each of her parents?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Cross: X^H X^h × X^H Y. Possible offspring: X^H X^H (normal female), X^H X^h (carrier female), X^H Y (normal male), X^h Y (affected male). (a) P(haemophilia, all children) = 1/4 = 25%. (b) P(haemophilia | son) = 1/2 = 50% — half of sons are affected. (c) P(haemophilia | daughter) = 0 — daughters receive an X^H from the father and either X^H or X^h from the mother; they may be carriers but not affected.

(2) Males have only one X chromosome (XY). A single copy of the recessive allele X^h on their one X chromosome is sufficient to cause haemophilia — there is no second X chromosome to provide a dominant X^H allele. Females (XX) would need two copies (X^h X^h) to be affected — they would need to inherit X^h from both parents. This requires the father to be affected (X^h Y) and the mother to be a carrier or affected — a much rarer combination. Therefore, X-linked recessives are overwhelmingly more common in males.

(3) Two possibilities: (a) Victoria's mother was a carrier (X^H X^h) — Victoria had a 50% chance of inheriting the X^h allele from her carrier mother, with neither grandparent being affected. (b) De novo mutation — a new mutation arose in one of Victoria's parents' gametes (most likely the egg, since more cell divisions occur in oogenesis over a lifetime). Both explanations are genetically valid; DNA analysis of preserved remains of her descendants suggests the de novo mutation hypothesis is more likely, as no carrier females have been identified in the preceding generations.

(4) X-linked conditions carried on the X chromosome — the X chromosome must come from the mother (sons receive X from mother, Y from father). A de novo mutation in haemophilia A would most likely arise in the egg (maternal gamete), since the son inherits his only X chromosome from his mother. If the mutation arose in the mother's germline (during oogenesis), the mother would be a mosaic carrier or simply a carrier for that gamete without being clinically affected herself, depending on timing. The Y chromosome from the father plays no role in X-linked traits.

(5) A girl with haemophilia A must be genotype X^h X^h. This requires: (a) Her father must be affected (X^h Y — he passes X^h to all daughters). (b) Her mother must be at least a carrier (X^H X^h) — passing X^h to this daughter. So: father has haemophilia, mother is a carrier (or also affected, though this is rarer). This is precisely why affected females are so rare — they require an affected father and a carrier or affected mother.
learningObjectives: Apply Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment to solve monohybrid and dihybrid cross problems using Punnett squares.
Explain extensions to Mendelian genetics including incomplete dominance, codominance, polygenic traits, and sex-linked inheritance.
Describe the molecular basis of mutations (point mutations, frameshifts, chromosomal), their causes, and consequences for protein function.
Explain how gene expression is regulated and describe key biotechnology tools (PCR, gel electrophoresis, CRISPR) and their applications.
commonMistakes: Applying the Law of Independent Assortment to linked genes — genes on the same chromosome are inherited together (linked) and do not assort independently; only genes on different chromosomes assort independently.

Assuming the gambler's fallacy applies to genetics — each conception is independent; having one affected child does not reduce the probability that the next child will be affected (still 25% for two carrier parents).

Confusing dominance with frequency — dominant alleles are not necessarily the most common in a population; recessive alleles can be very common (e.g. PKU is recessive but the allele frequency is significant).

Thinking dominant means 'stronger' or 'better' — dominance is a molecular interaction: a dominant allele produces a functional protein that is sufficient even in one copy; it has no special evolutionary advantage over recessives.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly constructs Punnett squares and calculates probabilities for monohybrid, dihybrid, and X-linked crosses.
Accurately explains extensions to Mendelian genetics (codominance, incomplete dominance, sex linkage) with appropriate examples.
Classifies mutation types, predicts their consequences for protein function, and explains their molecular basis.
Describes CRISPR-Cas9 mechanism and one application accurately; explains the principle of PCR and its uses in diagnostics or forensics.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve changes to the DNA sequence. Mechanisms include DNA methylation (typically silencing genes) and histone modification (acetylation activates, methylation can activate or repress). Epigenetic marks can be influenced by environment (nutrition, stress, toxins) and, in some cases, passed to offspring — the study of transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is active and controversial.

A mathematical model predicting allele and genotype frequencies in an idealised non-evolving population: p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p and q are frequencies of two alleles. The equilibrium holds only when there is no selection, mutation, genetic drift, gene flow, or non-random mating. Deviations from HWE indicate evolutionary forces are acting — it is used in population genetics and forensic statistics.

Genomic regions statistically associated with variation in a quantitative (continuous) trait such as height, blood pressure, or yield. Identified by genome-wide association studies (GWAS) that correlate millions of SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) with phenotypic data across thousands of individuals. Most complex diseases involve hundreds of QTLs of small effect.

Most organisms are diploid (2n — two copies of each chromosome). Polyploidy (more than two sets) is common in plants and is often the result of hybridisation followed by chromosome doubling. Many crop species are polyploid: bread wheat is hexaploid (6n = 42 chromosomes). Polyploidy can confer hybrid vigour and is important in plant breeding and evolutionary speciation.

DNA extracted from archaeological and palaeontological remains — teeth, bone, frozen tissue. aDNA analysis has revealed the genome sequences of Neanderthals and Denisovans, documented modern human migration out of Africa, identified ancient diseases, and shown that all non-African humans carry ≈1–4% Neanderthal DNA from ancient interbreeding. Requires specialised clean-room facilities to prevent modern DNA contamination.

questions.questionHtml: In a dihybrid cross between two pea plants heterozygous for seed colour (Y = yellow, y = green) and seed shape (R = round, r = wrinkled) — YyRr × YyRr — what is the expected proportion of offspring with yellow, wrinkled seeds?
questions.explanationHtml: The dihybrid cross gives a 9:3:3:1 ratio: 9 Y_R_ (yellow round) : 3 Y_rr (yellow wrinkled) : 3 yyR_ (green round) : 1 yyrr (green wrinkled). Yellow wrinkled = Y_rr = 3/16. Using the multiplication rule: P(yellow) = 3/4 × P(wrinkled) = 1/4 → 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16. This follows from Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment — the two genes are on different chromosomes and segregate independently.

questions.questionHtml: A woman of blood type A (genotype I^A i) and a man of blood type B (genotype I^B i) have children. Which blood types are possible in their offspring, and in what proportions?
options: A, B, AB, and O (1:1:1:1 ratio)
questions.correctAnswer: A, B, AB, and O (1:1:1:1 ratio)
questions.explanationHtml: Cross: I^A i × I^B i. Punnett square: I^A I^B (blood type AB), I^A i (blood type A), I^B i (blood type B), ii (blood type O) — each with probability 1/4. This cross can produce all four ABO blood types. I^A and I^B are codominant (both expressed in I^A I^B individuals), while i is recessive (ii gives type O — no A or B antigens). This is a classic example illustrating multiple alleles (three alleles: I^A, I^B, i) and codominance.

questions.questionHtml: CRISPR-Cas9 is used to correct a single base mutation causing a recessive genetic disease in a patient's somatic cells. A researcher claims this procedure will prevent the disease being passed to the patient's children. Evaluate this claim.
options: Correct — editing the patient's cells cures the disease in all tissues including germline cells

Incorrect — somatic cell gene editing affects only the treated body cells; it does not alter the DNA in the patient's germline (sperm or eggs) and therefore does not prevent inheritance of the mutation by offspring
Correct — but only if all somatic cells are successfully edited; partial editing would still allow transmission
Incorrect — CRISPR cannot target single base mutations; it only works on large insertions and deletions
questions.correctAnswer: Incorrect — somatic cell gene editing affects only the treated body cells; it does not alter the DNA in the patient's germline (sperm or eggs) and therefore does not prevent inheritance of the mutation by offspring
questions.explanationHtml: A critical distinction in gene therapy: somatic cell editing vs germline editing. Somatic cells are non-reproductive body cells (liver, blood, muscle, etc.). Editing somatic cells can treat or cure disease symptoms in the patient, but the edited cells cannot pass the correction to offspring — the patient's germline cells (sperm or eggs) still carry the original mutation. Germline editing — modifying the DNA of embryos, sperm, or eggs — would be heritable and could prevent transmission, but is controversial, subject to strict regulation, and largely prohibited in most countries for human applications (except research). The first reported human germline CRISPR edits (He Jiankui, 2018, in China) were widely condemned as premature and unethical. CRISPR can target single base pairs with appropriate guide RNA design and base editors — option D is incorrect.
